:::{#def-hazard}
#### Hazard function

The **hazard function** (also called the **hazard rate** or **hazard rate function**)
of a continuous random variable $T$ at a value $t$ with $\Pr(T \ge t) > 0$,
typically denoted $\haz(t)$ or $\h(t)$,
is the limit of the [conditional probability](probability-basics.qmd#def-conditional-prob)
that $T$ falls in an interval starting at $t$, given $T \ge t$,
divided by the width of that interval,
as that width shrinks to 0:

{{< include pds/_subfiles/_eq-def-hazard.qmd >}}

:::

::: {.remark .notes}

Sources differ on the symbol:
$\h(t)$ appears in
@dobson4e, @vittinghoff2e, @klein2003survival, and @kleinbaum2012survival,
while $\lambda(t)$ appears in
@me4 and @kalbfleisch2011statistical.

If $T$ is the time at which an event occurs,
then $\haz(t)$ is a rate, not a probability:
for a small interval width $\change > 0$,
$\haz(t) \cd \change$ is approximately the probability
that the event occurs in $[t, t + \change)$,
given that it has not occurred before $t$.
Many sources write the hazard as $\haz(t) = \p(T = t \mid T \ge t)$,
reading it as the density of $T$ at $t$, conditional on the event $T \ge t$;
that notation abbreviates the limit in @def-hazard.
For a discrete $T$, the analogous quantity is the
[discrete-time hazard](#def-discrete-hazard).

The name "hazard" carries a connotation that the event is undesirable ---
death, relapse, equipment failure, and so on.
When the event in question is neutral or desirable
(recovery, conception, graduation, response to treatment),
the same quantity $\haz(t)$ is often called the
**event incidence rate** instead.
This terminology parallels the convention that conditional probabilities of
undesirable events are called **risks**,
while the same conditional probabilities for neutral or desirable events
are simply called **probabilities**.
The math is identical; only the name changes with the valence of the event.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-hazard-exceeds-one}
#### A hazard greater than 1

A hazard can exceed 1, just as a density can (@exm-normal).
Let $T$ be [exponential](#def-exponential) with rate $\rate = 2$,
so $\surv(t) = \ef{-2t}$ for $t \ge 0$ (@exm-exp-survfn).
Since $T$ is continuous, $\Pr(T = s) = 0$ for every $s$,
so $\Pr(T \ge s) = \Pr(T > s) = \surv(s)$.
For $t \ge 0$ and $\change > 0$,
$\{T \ge t\}$ is the disjoint union of $\{t \le T < t + \change\}$ and $\{T \ge t + \change\}$,
so:

$$
\ba
\Pr(t \le T < t + \change \mid T \ge t)
&= \frac{\Pr(\{t \le T < t + \change\} \cap \{T \ge t\})}{\Pr(T \ge t)}
&& \text{(definition of conditional probability)} \\
&= \frac{\Pr(t \le T < t + \change)}{\Pr(T \ge t)}
&& \text{(subset property)} \\
&= \frac{\Pr(T \ge t) - \Pr(T \ge t + \change)}{\Pr(T \ge t)}
&& \text{(additivity)} \\
&= \frac{\surv(t) - \surv(t + \change)}{\surv(t)}
&& \text{(} \Pr(T \ge s) = \surv(s) \text{)} \\
&= \frac{\ef{-2t} - \ef{-2(t + \change)}}{\ef{-2t}}
&& \text{(exponential survival function)} \\
&= 1 - \ef{-2\change}
&& \text{(divide by } \ef{-2t} \text{)}
\ea
$$

The [subset property](probability-basics.qmd#thm-prob-subset) applies
because $\{t \le T < t + \change\} \subseteq \{T \ge t\}$.
Then:

$$
\ba
\haz(t)
&= \lim_{\change \downarrow 0} \frac{1 - \ef{-2\change}}{\change}
&& \text{(definition of the hazard function)} \\
&= \evalAt{\deriv{\change} \paren{1 - \ef{-2\change}}}{\change = 0}
&& \text{(definition of the derivative; } 1 - \ef{0} = 0 \text{)} \\
&= 2\ef{0}
&& \text{(chain rule)} \\
&= 2
&& \text{(} \ef{0} = 1 \text{)}
\ea
$$

So $\haz(t) = 2 > 1$ at every $t \ge 0$:
a hazard is a rate, not a probability.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-discrete-hazard}
#### Discrete-time hazard

The **discrete-time hazard** of a [discrete](#def-discrete-rv) random variable $T$
at a value $t$ with $\Pr(T \ge t) > 0$
is the [conditional probability](probability-basics.qmd#def-conditional-prob)
that $T$ equals $t$, given $T \ge t$:

$$\Pr(T = t \mid T \ge t)$$

:::

:::{#exm-discrete-hazard}
#### Rolling until the first six

Roll a fair die repeatedly,
and let $T$ be the number of the roll that first shows a six.
Then $T \ge t$ exactly when the first $t - 1$ rolls are not sixes,
which has probability $(5/6)^{t-1}$,
and $T = t$ when, in addition, roll $t$ is a six.
So, for each $t = 1, 2, \ldots$:

$$
\ba
\Pr(T = t \mid T \ge t)
&= \frac{\Pr(T = t,\, T \ge t)}{\Pr(T \ge t)}
&& \text{(definition of conditional probability)} \\
&= \frac{\Pr(T = t)}{\Pr(T \ge t)}
&& \text{(} T = t \text{ implies } T \ge t \text{)} \\
&= \frac{(5/6)^{t-1} \cd (1/6)}{(5/6)^{t-1}}
&& \text{(rolls are independent)} \\
&= \frac{1}{6}
&& \text{(cancel)}
\ea
$$

The discrete-time hazard is the same at every roll:
having gone without a six so far does not change the chance of a six on the next roll.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#cor-discrete-hazard-unit-interval}
#### A discrete-time hazard lies in ${[0, 1]}$

The [discrete-time hazard](#def-discrete-hazard) of a discrete random variable $T$
at a value $t$ with $\Pr(T \ge t) > 0$ satisfies:

$$0 \le \Pr(T = t \mid T \ge t) \le 1$$

:::

::: proof

$\{T \ge t\}$ is the disjoint union of $\{T = t\}$ and $\{T > t\}$,
so, by additivity, $\Pr(T \ge t) = \Pr(T = t) + \Pr(T > t) \ge \Pr(T = t)$.
Since $\{T = t\} \subseteq \{T \ge t\}$:

$$
\ba
\Pr(T = t \mid T \ge t)
&= \frac{\Pr(\{T = t\} \cap \{T \ge t\})}{\Pr(T \ge t)}
&& \text{(definition of conditional probability)} \\
&= \frac{\Pr(T = t)}{\Pr(T \ge t)}
&& \text{(subset property)}
\ea
$$

The numerator is non-negative and at most the positive denominator,
so the ratio lies in $[0, 1]$.

:::

::: {.remark .notes}

Unlike the continuous-time [hazard function](#def-hazard),
which is a rate and can exceed 1 (@exm-hazard-exceeds-one),
the discrete-time hazard is a probability.

:::
